note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — STREAMING RIBBON LEAVES
tiles.details: Noncontact sight recognition: long current-streaming leaves appear in Joey panel 3 (index 2), USFWS underwater habitat panel 6 (index 5), and the two authentic USFWS river panoramas in panels 7–8 (indices 6–7). All are source-identified Texas wild-rice in the San Marcos river; none exposes rootstock or the true leaf collar. The species is federally AND state endangered. Never enter, touch, pull or move wild material just for identification photos.
tiles.short: Protected aquatic perennial: long submerged ribbons flowing with the river current.
tiles.status: STREAMING HABIT AND RIVER PATCHES PHOTOGRAPHED — ROOTED BASE NOT EXPOSED

tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE COLLAR — A DOCUMENTED PHOTO GAP
tiles.details: Published grass treatment describes an INNER 5–15 mm MEMBRANOUS ligule at actual blade–sheath junction, not merely the central leaf vein or water droplet. Current gallery has NO approved pixel-level true inner ligule view. Do not touch a protected wild blade or dig up a crown. Request or license an already photographed conservation-cultivated plant at San Marcos Aquatic Resources Center / approved partner; make an ex-situ subject identity explicit.
tiles.short: Published membranous ligule 5–15 mm; root growth perennial; collar unverified in gallery.
tiles.status: REFERENCED MEMBRANOUS LIGULE 5–15 MM — NO VALIDATED PHOTO, NO WILD HANDLING

tiles.heading: 03 · MALE LOWER / FEMALE UPPER BRANCHES
tiles.details: Panels 2, 4–5 (indices 1,3,4) show true hanging pollen-bearing ANTHERS, not female lemma awns; the newly archived USFWS flowering-shoot photo panel 9 (index 8) shows many connected branch positions while panel 10 (index 9) has elongated green female-looking units plus yellow hanging parts. The expected botanical sex map: LOWER spreading male branches versus UPPER more ascending female branches. An individual complete head with specifically verified branch origins and sex is STILL missing; overlapping shoots are not evidence of a confidently mapped entire individual.
tiles.short: Panicle ~20–30 cm: spreading lower male branches; ascending upper female branches.
tiles.status: NEW MIXED FLOWERING ARCHITECTURE PHOTO — PRECISE FEMALE/MALE BRANCH ORIGINS OPEN

tiles.heading: 04 · MALE SPIKELET — AWNLESS, GLUMES ABSENT
tiles.details: On existing Joey and USFWS photos 2/4/5 (indices 1,3,4), individual hanging yellow male ANTHERS can be recognized; whole spikelet length ~7–9 mm and five-veined awnless male lemma remain SOURCE ranges, not photo measurements. Actual paired glumes are absent in Zizania. The new photo panel 10 (index 9) has mixed sex-looking forms but does not identify complete male glumes/lemma boundaries, and is NOT a voucher or safe scale for microscopic anatomy.
tiles.short: Male spikelets ~7–9 mm; five-veined lemma; no long awn.

tiles.heading: 05 · FEMALE SPIKELET — ONE TERMINAL LEMMA AWN
tiles.details: NEW USFWS panel 10 (index 9) shows a cluster of slender upright green seed-bearing/awn-like units and separate pendant pale flowers, and panel 9 (index 8) places them in a fuller panicle context. These are candidate visual female features, but NO scale or resolved attachment point proves one terminal awn from the FEMALE lemma. Published female spikelet ~10 mm, lemma awn ~10–20 (sometimes ~25) mm, and ordinary paired glumes absent; labels on that precise insertion are withheld until a verifiable authorized cultivated research photo is available.
tiles.short: Female spikelet ~10 mm; 3-veined lemma; one 10–20(–25) mm awn.
tiles.status: CANDIDATE FEMALE-AWNED UNITS NOW PHOTOGRAPHED — SOURCE-SCALED LEMMA ATTACHMENT UNRESOLVED

tiles.heading: 06 · LOOK-ALIKES AND PUBLIC-READY GATE
tiles.details: TWO real DIFFERENT species photos are now shown: giant cutgrass (*Zizaniopsis miliacea*) in panel 11 (index 10), and rice cutgrass (*Leersia oryzoides*) in panel 12 (index 11). Do not call either wild rice. Exactly TEN own-species archived photos show flowing habitat and male flowers plus new branching head/awned-looking units; none proves lifted root/stolon/crown or true inner membranous ligule. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: existing authorized conservation-grown ROOT photo, true opened ligule without wild contact, one truly connected panicle with scientifically sexed LOWER male/UPPER female branches and a clear terminal female lemma awn. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify noncommercial Joey photo-level CC BY-NC rights, all public-domain USFWS credits, CC BY/BY-SA comparison attribution, 12 actual panels and the existing 11 gross arrows; live web and mobile must be checked separately.
tiles.short: Field-ready no-contact lesson, but complete protected-species anatomy and public-site QA remain held.
tiles.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — NO WILD HANDLING; WEBSITE QA UNCONFIRMED

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: TEXAS WILD-RICE (*Zizania texana*) — ENDANGERED. See long submerged ribbonlike leaves streaming in upper San Marcos River; actual USFWS river photographs cover this gross habit. At flowering, LOWER spreading branches bear pendent awnless staminate units/anthers; UPPER more ascending branches produce slender awned pistillate spikelets. NEW USFWS gallery panels 9–10 now show flowering branch architecture and awned-looking green units, but do NOT prove exact individual female lemma awn or continuous same-panicle sex map. Both actual underwater ROOTED CROWN and 5–15mm true inner membranous LIGULE are STILL missing; acquire only authorized existing ex-situ conservation photographs, never manipulate wild endangered plants. Look-alikes Zizaniopsis miliacea and Leersia oryzoides now have clearly labeled source-licensed comparison photographs.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: FIRST observe from a permitted, non-intrusive place without touching or entering a protected stand. New public-domain USFWS panel 11 (index10) shows genuinely long submerged ribbon blades streaming with current and one upright flowering stem. Neither the current nor visible sediment proves an exposed attached root.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Published grass treatment describes an INNER 5–15 mm MEMBRANOUS ligule at actual blade–sheath junction, not merely the central leaf vein or water droplet. Current gallery has NO approved pixel-level true inner ligule view. Do not touch a protected wild blade or dig up a crown. Request or license an already photographed conservation-cultivated plant at San Marcos Aquatic Resources Center / approved partner; make an ex-situ subject identity explicit.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: On existing Joey and USFWS photos 2/4/5 (indices 1,3,4), individual hanging yellow male ANTHERS can be recognized; whole spikelet length ~7–9 mm and five-veined awnless male lemma remain SOURCE ranges, not photo measurements. Actual paired glumes are absent in Zizania. The new photo panel 10 (index 9) has mixed sex-looking forms but does not identify complete male glumes/lemma boundaries, and is NOT a voucher or safe scale for microscopic anatomy.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Zizaniopsis miliacea/giant cutgrass grows in large emergent reedlike marsh clumps with a broad airy panicle; Leersia oryzoides has scratchy leaf edges and rice-like one-flowered spikelets, but is not equivalent to rare Texas wild-rice. Use precise live river habitat plus leaf/inflorescence anatomy and expert determination; no invasive management or routine native planting recommendations.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

memory_rule: TEXAS WILD-RICE (*Zizania texana*) is a federally/state ENDANGERED aquatic perennial endemic to the upper San Marcos River in Hays County. Long ribbonlike underwater leaves align with current; flowering shoots can emerge. Species bears separate male and female flowers arranged on branching flowerhead sections. This source photo shows yellow anthers on a flowering spray. Observe only—NEVER pull, harvest, transplant, or trample; photograph from permitted positions.
safety_note: Federally/state endangered San Marcos River endemic. Only noncontact view and existing authorized federal research photos. 13 own-species archived original photos, 15 teaching panels including 2 different-species comparator; 20 gross arrows. No GPS for protected stands; rootstock or true inner ligule remains missing. Photographic completeness 3.5/6 (58%), NOT an endorsement of collection or a 100% field-ID determination.
field_rule: Identify endangered Texas wild-rice from legally permitted observation only: ribbon leaves streaming in running water, emerge a flowering axis, follow top ascending female-bearing and lower spreading male-bearing floral regions with dangling anthers. Final uncertain identifications belong to authorized botanical specialists. Do not touch/enter/collect protected plants.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: Zizaniopsis miliacea/giant cutgrass grows in large emergent reedlike marsh clumps with a broad airy panicle; Leersia oryzoides has scratchy leaf edges and rice-like one-flowered spikelets, but is not equivalent to rare Texas wild-rice. Use precise live river habitat plus leaf/inflorescence anatomy and expert determination; no invasive management or routine native planting recommendations.
